source.title: When do data mixtures improve scaling laws? Insights from high-dimensional regression
source.authors: Diyuan Wu; Lehan Chen; Theodor Misiakiewicz; Marco Mondelli

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures target-domain held-out NLL across token budgets in language-model data-mixture experiments, using a fixed-size model and different scaling fits from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The paper also gives theoretical and numerical regression scaling results, but those are not rows for language-model scaling claims. The language-model evidence includes a fixed-size GPT-2-style model and token-budget sweeps; it does not vary parameter count or training compute. Figure 3 gives qualitative comparisons, while Table 1 reports OLS slopes for a close-distribution mixture.
record.test_reason: The only language-model evidence that bears on a version is V7. With a fixed 81.5M GPT-2-style model, the slope of target-domain NLL against log target budget changes with training-data composition (target-only, auxiliary, mixture). This is a weak, data-only test of fit-dependence. It does not test V1: the token range is about 5x (4–20M), and the fit is NLL linear in ln(n), not a power law. Parameters and compute are not varied. The regression theory and the CIFAR/ImageNet ridge experiments are not language-model scaling results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. One correction: for close distributions the authors say mixtures do not improve scaling over a single dataset 'across different scales γ2'. Yet Table 1 shows the mixture slope steeper than both single sources at γ2=0.75 and 1 (+5.1%/+43.7%, +23.5%/+22.4%). Only at γ2≥1.25 does the mixture fail to beat auxiliary-only.
record.recipe_differences: The language-model experiment holds model size fixed at 81.5M parameters and varies target and auxiliary token budgets and their mixture; it does not use a joint parameter, token, and compute scaling sweep or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The mixture outcome changes with auxiliary-to-target token growth rate (gamma2) and with similarity of the target and auxiliary token-frequency distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing target and auxiliary text yields a faster target-domain NLL decrease than either source alone only within a window of relative growth γ2. The authors link this to the auxiliary source covering tokens rare in the target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-mixture composition and relative source growth can change the scaling rate of target-domain loss with target-data budget.

record.problems: The language-model study uses one model size, a limited token-budget range, and six target-budget values; Table 1 averages slopes over three seeds but reports no uncertainty. The reported OLS fit is NLL against ln(token budget), not a direct test of the claimed power-law loss form. The Figure 3 numerical values are available only graphically.

untested.parts: No power-law form is fitted (NLL linear in ln n). The range is about 5x in tokens. Parameters and compute are not varied.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Text pretraining only. Data mixing is not repetition, fine-tuning or transfer.
Parameter counting, schedule choice, fitting method, comparison of published exponents, compute-optimal split and curvature away from a power law are all untested. Only data composition is varied.

missing.what: Figure 4(a): close-distribution mixture at γ2=1.25 vs target-only and auxiliary-only curves. The authors say the mixture gives no improvement.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 limits_scope label is dropped: a log-linear fit over 5x in tokens cannot bear on a multi-decade power law. Target-only rows are one result repeated six times. Auxiliary-only and γ2>1 mixture slopes are regressed on target budget n while their own tokens grow as n^γ2, so cross-condition slope comparisons are partly axis artifacts. Learning-rate schedule length also changes with total tokens. The study is a preprint with no seed uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Only token-budget variation at fixed model size is examined. The experiments do not establish a power law in loss itself, test parameter-count or compute scaling, cover several orders of magnitude, or establish the non-bottleneck conditions in the claim.
The study does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on substantially larger runs.
The experiments vary relative target and auxiliary token growth, but do not optimize parameter and token counts under a fixed compute budget.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architectures at fixed parameter count is reported.
The language-model experiments concern text pretraining, not other modalities, repetition, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Target-domain test NLL is reported, but the study does not evaluate downstream tasks or predict downstream performance.

The study tests sensitivity to domain-mixture composition and relative token growth. It does not vary parameter-counting conventions or fitting methods, compare published exponents, investigate compute-optimal parameter/token splits, or test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: 81.5M-parameter GPT-2-style model
rows.operation_detail: Fit target test NLL = alpha + s ln(n) for target-only training.
rows.measure: OLS slope s of target test NLL against ln(target dataset size)
rows.note: The negative slope indicates declining NLL with target budget. The reported fit is NLL linear in ln(n), not a direct fit of a power law in loss.
rows.check: Comparator only. Target-only runs are identical across γ2, so T1, T4, T7, T10, T13 and T16 are the same value (-0.8319) repeated. One row would do. A 5x range with an NLL-vs-ln(n) fit cannot show V1's power law.

rows.measure: OLS slope s of target test NLL against ln(target dataset size)
rows.note: The negative slope indicates declining NLL with target budget. The reported fit is NLL linear in ln(n), not a direct fit of a power law in loss.
rows.check: Auxiliary-only slope is regressed on the target budget n, while auxiliary tokens grow as n^γ2. The slope therefore scales roughly with γ2 by construction. Per auxiliary token it is about -0.81 to -0.93, close to target-only.

relationships.condition: Fixed 81.5M model. Close-distribution mixture at γ2=1, and OOD mixture at γ2=1.25 (figure/text only).
relationships.reason: The target-loss rate depends on training-data composition (T6: -1.03 vs -0.83 target-only; F1 text). Evidence is weak: 5x range, log-linear slopes, no uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: A data mixture yielded a target-loss slope of −1.03 versus −0.83 for target-only training, measured over a fivefold range without uncertainty estimates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fixed 81.5M model and the reported target-token ranges
reader_labels.reason: The negative slopes show falling target NLL, but the paper fits NLL linearly against ln(n), over a limited token range; it does not establish the claimed power-law loss form or other scaling axes. Rows T1-T18.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OOD-mixture growth settings and close-distribution mixtures across the tested gamma2 values
reader_labels.reason: The OOD-mixture improvement is reported only at gamma2 = 1.25, while the authors say it is not noticeable at 0.75 or 1.75; the close-distribution slopes also vary in their comparison with single-domain slopes across settings. Rows F1-F3 and T1-T18.
